SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
Answers and Solutions  
1. Answer B  
Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, the concept of an “insider” is  
deliberately framed very broadly, and Option B correctly captures the essence of this definition.  
Regulation 2(1)(g) defines an insider as any person who is either (i) a connected person, or (ii)  
in possession of or having access to unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI). The use of  
the word “or” is critical and establishes the possession-based test as an independent ground for  
insider status. Therefore, even if a person has no formal, contractual, or employment-based  
relationship with the company, mere access to UPSI is sufficient to bring that person within the  
regulatory net. SEBI consciously moved away from a purely relationship-based test because  
insider trading often occurs through informal channels, leaks, or indirect access. Courts and  
SEBI adjudicating officers have consistently emphasised that insider trading regulations are  
preventive in nature and must be interpreted expansively to protect market integrity. Once a  
person has access to UPSI, the law presumes the ability to misuse it, irrespective of designation  
or shareholding. Option A is incorrect because shareholding percentage has no bearing on  
insider status under the PIT Regulations. Option C is incorrect because even junior employees  
may have access to UPSI depending on their role. Option D is overly restrictive and legally  
unsustainable, as company secretaries are only one category of connected persons. Option E is  
irrelevant because accounting classification as a related party does not automatically confer  
insider status unless UPSI access is established. Thus, Option B correctly reflects the  
possession-based approach embedded in the 2015 Regulations.  
2. Answer C  
Option C is correct because the 2018 amendment to the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations, 2015, specifically introduced Regulation 3(2B), which fundamentally altered how  
recipients of UPSI are treated. Prior to this amendment, there was ambiguity regarding whether  
persons receiving UPSI for legitimate purposes could still be considered insiders. Regulation  
3(2B) clarifies that any person who receives UPSI pursuant to a legitimate purpose shall be  
considered an insider, even though the communication itself may be lawful. The rationale  
behind this provision is rooted in risk management rather than moral culpability. SEBI  
recognises that certain disclosures of UPSI are commercially unavoidable, such as disclosures  
to auditors, legal advisors, insolvency professionals, or strategic partners. However, once UPSI  
is shared, the recipient is placed in a position of informational advantage. To prevent misuse,  
the law imposes insider obligations on such recipients, including restrictions on trading and  
further communication. Option A is incorrect because receiving UPSI does not convert a person  
into a promoter or deemed promoter. Option B is incorrect because whistleblowers operate  
under a different regulatory framework and are not automatically classified under Regulation  
3(2B). Option D is incorrect because insider status does not depend on payroll or employment.  
16  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
Option E is directly contrary to the regulation, as recipients of UPSI are expressly included  
17  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
within the insider definition, not excluded. Therefore, Option C accurately reflects the legal  
consequence of receiving UPSI for legitimate purposes after the 2018 amendment.  
3. Answer B  
Option B correctly defines “unpublished price sensitive information” (UPSI) under Regulation  
2(1)(n) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. UPSI is information that is  
not generally available and which, upon becoming generally available, is likely to materially  
affect the price of securities. Both elements must coexist. If information is price sensitive but  
already public, it ceases to be UPSI. Conversely, confidential information that has no price  
impact also falls outside UPSI. SEBI provides an inclusive list of examples such as financial  
results, dividends, mergers, acquisitions, changes in capital structure, and key managerial  
decisions. The emphasis on “material” impact ensures that trivial or speculative information is  
excluded, while significant corporate developments are covered. Option A is incorrect because  
information that is publicly available cannot be UPSI, regardless of price impact. Option C is  
incorrect because UPSI is not restricted to promoters’ knowledge; employees, advisors, and  
third parties may possess it. Option D is incorrect because forward-looking statements disclosed  
to analysts, if properly disclosed publicly, form part of generally available information. Option E  
is incorrect because mere circulation on private WhatsApp groups does not make information  
public; however, not all such information qualifies as UPSI unless price sensitivity is established.  
Thus, Option B accurately captures the statutory definition and regulatory intent behind UPSI.  
4. Answer C  
Option C is correct because “generally available information” under Regulation 2(1)(e) refers to  
information that is accessible to the public on a non-discriminatory basis. The core idea is  
equality of access. Information must be disseminated in a manner that allows all investors an  
equal opportunity to receive and assess it, such as through stock exchange disclosures, press  
releases, or widely circulated media reports. SEBI has repeatedly clarified that selective  
disclosure undermines market fairness and violates the principle of equal access. Even if  
information is accurate and truthful, it does not become generally available unless it is disclosed  
through recognised public channels. Option A is incorrect because selective sharing with  
lenders does not satisfy public accessibility. Option B is incorrect because disclosure limited to  
merchant bankers remains restricted. Option D is incorrect because internal discussions among  
employees are, by definition, non-public. Option E is incorrect because private investor calls  
limit access to a select group and do not qualify as public dissemination unless simultaneously  
made available to the entire market. Therefore, Option C aligns with both the text of the  
regulation and SEBI’s emphasis on non-discriminatory information flow.  
5. Answer A  
Option A correctly reflects the definition of a “connected person” under Regulation 2(1)(d) of the  
SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. A connected person includes anyone  
who is or has been associated with the company, directly or indirectly, during the six months  
18  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
prior to the relevant act, in any capacity that allows access to UPSI. This includes employment,  
19  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
professional engagement, contractual relationships, or fiduciary roles. The six-month look-back  
period is critical. SEBI recognises that access to UPSI does not end abruptly upon resignation  
or termination. Former employees, consultants, or advisors may continue to possess sensitive  
information that remains unpublished. Therefore, the law presumes access during this  
cooling-off period. Option B is incorrect because mere trading activity does not establish a  
connection. Option C is incorrect because small shareholding does not imply access to UPSI.  
Option D is incorrect because ordinary customers typically lack access to internal information.  
Option E is incorrect because the definition operates automatically and does not depend on  
SEBI issuing individual notifications. Hence, Option A correctly captures the temporal and  
relational scope of a connected person.  
6. Answer B  
Option B is correct because the substituted Regulation 3(5), introduced through the 2020  
amendment to the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, mandates the  
maintenance of a structured digital database (SDD) internally, with robust safeguards such as  
time-stamping, audit trails, and non-tamperability. The purpose of this requirement is to create  
accountability and traceability for the flow of UPSI within and outside the organisation. The SDD  
must record details of persons with whom UPSI is shared, including names, PAN or other  
identifiers, and the date and time of sharing. This enables SEBI to reconstruct information trails  
during investigations and identify the source of leaks. Internal maintenance is crucial because  
outsourcing could dilute control, compromise confidentiality, and weaken evidentiary value.  
Option A is incorrect because the regulation does not permit outsourcing as a default  
mechanism. Option C is incorrect because maintaining an SDD is mandatory, not voluntary.  
Option D is incorrect because intermediaries and fiduciaries are also required to maintain such  
databases. Option E is incorrect because the obligation is continuous and not limited to trading  
windows. Thus, Option B accurately reflects the compliance architecture envisaged by SEBI to  
strengthen insider trading enforcement.  
7. Answer B  
Option B is correct because the 2018 amendment to the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations, 2015, formally recognised “legitimate purpose” as a valid ground for  
communicating UPSI, and expressly includes sharing such information with partners, auditors,  
insolvency professionals, merchant bankers, legal advisors, and similar fiduciaries. These  
disclosures are often necessary for audits, due diligence, restructuring, or statutory compliance.  
However, SEBI balances commercial necessity with regulatory caution. While such sharing is  
permitted, it does not dilute the confidentiality obligations attached to UPSI. Recipients are  
treated as insiders, required to maintain confidentiality, and prohibited from trading or further  
communicating the information except for the same legitimate purpose. Option A is incorrect  
because marketing agencies do not ordinarily require UPSI. Option C is incorrect because  
influencers serve promotional, not fiduciary, roles. Option D is incorrect because advertisement  
departments do not require confidential corporate information. Option E is incorrect because  
sharing UPSI for academic or training purposes would defeat the purpose of confidentiality.  
20  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
Therefore, Option B correctly reflects SEBI’s narrow and functional interpretation of “legitimate  
purpose.”  
8. Answer C  
Option C is correct because selectively disclosed information to analysts does not qualify as  
“generally available information” under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations,  
2015. Even if analysts are market intermediaries, selective disclosure creates informational  
asymmetry and violates the principle of equal access. SEBI has consistently acted against  
selective analyst briefings that convey material non-public information. Unless the same  
information is simultaneously disclosed to the public through stock exchanges or press  
releases, it remains unpublished. Options A, B, D, and E all involve public dissemination  
through recognised channels, making the information accessible to all investors. Therefore, they  
qualify as generally available information. Hence, Option C is the correct answer.  
9. Answer B  
Option B is correct because the 2025 amendment to the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations mandates that externally received UPSI must be entered into the structured digital  
database within two calendar days of receipt. This amendment was introduced to close  
loopholes relating to delayed or post-facto record-keeping. The rationale is that external sources  
such as advisors, consultants, or counterparties often become channels of information leakage.  
Timely entry ensures contemporaneous documentation, reducing the risk of manipulation or  
retrospective alteration. Options A, C, D, and E are incorrect because they either impose  
unrealistic immediacy, permit excessive delay, or make compliance contingent on SEBI  
intervention, which defeats the preventive objective of the regulation. Thus, Option B is legally  
accurate.  
10. Answer B  
Option B is correct because the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, adopt a  
possession-based standard. A person who trades while in possession of UPSI violates the  
regulations regardless of whether the trade is executed for their own benefit or on behalf of  
another. SEBI has repeatedly clarified that acting as an agent, portfolio manager, or  
intermediary does not provide immunity. The focus is on the act of trading while in possession of  
UPSI, not on who ultimately benefits. Options A, C, D, and E incorrectly attempt to carve out  
exemptions that do not exist in law. Therefore, Option B correctly states the legal position.  
11. Answer C  
Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, the definition of “insider” is  
deliberately framed in a disjunctive and expansive manner, and Option C correctly reflects this  
structure. Regulation 2(1)(g) provides that an insider means any person who is either a  
connected person OR is in possession of or having access to unpublished price sensitive  
21  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
information (UPSI). The use of the word “or” is legally significant and establishes two  
22  
SEBI (PIT) - MCQ  
independent gateways through which a person may qualify as an insider. The first limb,  
“connected person,” focuses on the relationship test. It covers individuals who, by virtue of their  
association with the company (present or past), are reasonably expected to have access to  
UPSI. The second limb is the possession-based test, which does not require any formal or  
contractual connection with the company. A person who acquires UPSI through informal,  
indirect, or even accidental means can still be treated as an insider. Option A is incorrect  
because possession of UPSI alone is sufficient, but the regulation does not limit insider status  
only to possession cases. Option B is incorrect because connection alone, even without proven  
possession, can trigger insider status due to presumed access. Option D is incorrect as  
promoters are merely a subset of insiders, not the exclusive category. Option E is incorrect  
because access to financial statements is only one possible form of UPSI access, not a defining  
criterion. Therefore, Option C accurately captures the dual test embedded in the statutory  
definition and reflects SEBI’s intent to prevent circumvention of insider trading laws.  
12. Answer B  
Option B is correct because quarterly financial results, until they are formally disclosed to the  
public through recognised channels, constitute unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI)  
under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. Regulation 2(1)(n) explicitly  
includes “financial results” as a category of information that is deemed price sensitive due to its  
direct and material impact on the market price of securities. In the given scenario, the company  
plans to disclose its quarterly results in five days. During this interim period, the information is  
clearly not generally available and remains confined to internal management, auditors, and  
select insiders. Since such results can significantly influence investor decisions and market  
valuation, they squarely fall within the definition of UPSI until official disclosure. Option A is  
incorrect because information does not become public merely because it is scheduled for  
disclosure. Option C is incorrect because “trading window information” is not a legal category  
under the regulations; trading window closures are compliance mechanisms, not classifications  
of information. Option D is incorrect because quarterly results are not routine disclosures in the  
sense of being continuously available; they are periodic and market-sensitive. Option E is  
incorrect because selective disclosure would imply partial sharing, which has not occurred in  
this scenario. Accordingly, Option B correctly reflects both the statutory language and SEBI’s  
consistent enforcement approach regarding financial disclosures.  
13. Answer E  
Option E is correct because an employee who has resigned yesterday without access to UPSI  
is not mandatorily treated as a connected person under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations, 2015. While Regulation 2(1)(d) includes past employees within the scope of  
connected persons for a period of six months after cessation of association, this inclusion is not  
absolute. The key qualifying element is whether the nature of the association was such that it  
allowed access to UPSI. SEBI’s framework is based on a presumption of access, not a blanket  
rule. If an employee’s role was clerical, operational, or otherwise insulated from sensitive

decision-making, and there is no factual basis to suggest access to UPSI, such a person may  
fall outside the mandatory connected person category.  
Options A, B, C, and D are incorrect because immediate relatives, auditors, bankers, and  
debenture trustees are explicitly recognised as connected persons due to the fiduciary nature of  
their roles and the inherent likelihood of access to sensitive information. Their inclusion is based  
on functional necessity rather than actual proof of access. Thus, Option E is correct because it  
recognises that mere past employment, without UPSI access, does not automatically result in  
insider classification, preserving proportionality and fairness in enforcement.  
14. Answer B  
Option B is correct because Regulation 4(1) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations, 2015 permits the communication of UPSI only when such communication is in  
furtherance of legitimate purposes, performance of duties, or discharge of legal obligations. This  
provision is an exception to the general prohibition on communication of UPSI and must be  
interpreted narrowly. Legitimate purpose refers to disclosures that are commercially or legally  
necessary, such as sharing information with auditors for statutory audits, legal advisors for  
compliance, or potential investors during due diligence. Even in such cases, the communication  
must be strictly limited, recorded, and subject to confidentiality obligations. Option A is incorrect  
because subjective belief about harmlessness has no legal relevance. Option C is incorrect  
because investor benefit is achieved through public disclosure, not private communication.  
Option D is incorrect because confidentiality agreements alone do not legalise communication  
unless the underlying purpose is legitimate. Option E is incorrect because oral disclosures are  
equally prohibited unless justified by legitimate purpose. Therefore, Option B accurately reflects  
the only lawful gateway through which UPSI may be communicated under the Regulations.  
15. Answer C  
Option C is correct because Regulation 5(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations, 2015 mandates that a trading plan shall commence only after a cooling-off period  
of at least six months from the date of public disclosure of the plan (which has now been  
changed to 120 days in the 2024 amendment). This cooling-off period is designed to  
neutralise any informational advantage the insider may possess at the time of formulating the  
plan. The trading plan mechanism exists to allow insiders to trade in a compliant manner while  
avoiding allegations of insider trading. However, SEBI imposes strict safeguards to prevent  
misuse. The six-month cooling-off period ensures that any UPSI known at the time of plan  
formulation is likely to become stale or publicly disclosed by the time trading begins. Option A is  
incorrect because there is no seven-day minimum period. Option B is incorrect because while  
trading plans may extend up to twelve months, this is not the defining requirement. Option D is  
incorrect because trading plans cannot be modified arbitrarily; any modification triggers a fresh  
cooling-off period. Option E is incorrect because trading plans must be disclosed to stock  
exchanges for transparency. Hence, Option C correctly captures the mandatory temporal  
safeguard governing trading plans.

Regulation 7 of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 prescribes  
disclosure obligations for promoters, members of the promoter group, designated persons, and  
directors when trading thresholds are crossed. Specifically, Regulation 7(2) mandates that every  
promoter, member of promoter group, and designated person shall disclose to the company the  
number of securities acquired or disposed of if the value of such trade exceeds ₹10 lakh in a  
calendar quarter. This disclosure obligation is transaction-value based and not contingent on  
whether the transaction is on-market or off-market. Option b) ₹10 lakh is therefore correct  
because SEBI consciously fixed this threshold to strike a balance between transparency and  
regulatory burden. Smaller trades are excluded to avoid excessive compliance, while material  
trades that may signal insider activity are captured. Option a) ₹5 lakh is incorrect because SEBI  
raised the threshold from earlier regimes to ₹10 lakh to reduce over-reporting. Option c) ₹25 lakh  
and option d) ₹50 lakh are incorrect as no such higher thresholds exist under Regulation 7.  
Option e) is incorrect because the regulation explicitly provides a quantified monetary trigger,  
contradicting the claim that no threshold applies. Thus, the correct statutory trigger for promoter  
disclosure is ₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter, making option b legally accurate.  
17. Answer B  
Regulation 2(1)(c) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 defines a  
“Compliance Officer” as a senior officer of the listed entity who is financially literate and capable  
of appreciating requirements for legal and regulatory compliance, and who shall report to the  
board of directors. The emphasis here is not on designation but on seniority, authority, and  
reporting structure. Option b is correct because SEBI intentionally avoided limiting the role to a  
specific profession. The Compliance Officer must have sufficient organizational authority to  
enforce trading window closures, approve trading plans, monitor disclosures, and ensure  
internal compliance. Reporting to the board ensures independence and effectiveness. Option a)  
is incorrect because a Compliance Officer need not be a company secretary only; CFOs, legal  
heads, or senior executives may also be appointed. Option c) is incorrect as promoter  
representatives may create conflicts of interest. Option d) is incorrect because shareholders  
have no role in such appointments. Option e) is incorrect because all listed companies, not only  
top 100, must appoint a Compliance Officer. Therefore, the defining legal requirement is  
seniority with board-level reporting, making option b correct.  
18. Answer C  
The Regulatory Sandbox framework introduced through amendments in 2020 and 2021 allows  
SEBI to relax certain regulatory provisions to facilitate innovation, testing of new market  
solutions, and regulatory experimentation. Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading)  
Regulations, this sandbox mechanism is incorporated via enabling provisions such as  
Regulation 31A and allied circulars. Option c) 12 months is correct because SEBI has explicitly  
capped exemptions granted under the sandbox framework at a maximum of one year, subject to  
conditions, monitoring, and revocation if misuse is detected. This temporal limitation reflects  
SEBI’s cautious approach: innovation is encouraged, but not at the cost of market integrity.  
Option a) 3 months and option b) 6 months are incorrect as they underestimate the permissible

19. Answer B  
Under Regulation 7 read with Schedule B (Code of Conduct) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider  
Trading) Regulations, 2015, pre-clearance of trades is required for designated persons only  
when the proposed trade exceeds a threshold specified in the Code of Conduct. Importantly,  
SEBI does not prescribe a uniform monetary figure. Option b is correct because the Compliance  
Officer determines the threshold, subject to board-approved internal policy. This allows flexibility  
based on company size, share price, liquidity, and risk profile. Option a) is incorrect because  
SEBI has intentionally avoided fixing a universal monetary limit. Option c) ₹1 lakh is incorrect as  
it is neither mandated nor standard. Option d) is incorrect because not all trades require  
pre-clearance; only those above the specified threshold do. Option e) is incorrect because stock  
exchanges do not determine internal compliance thresholds. Therefore, pre-clearance  
requirements are entity-specific and Compliance Officer-driven, making option b correct.  
20. Answer D  
Regulation 2(1)(n) defines Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) as information that is  
not generally available and which, upon becoming generally available, is likely to materially  
affect the price of securities. The regulation lists illustrative categories such as financial results,  
dividends, changes in capital structure, and expansion plans.  
Option d is correct because market rumors, even if published in newspapers or media, do not  
constitute UPSI unless they are confirmed or originate from the company. SEBI has consistently  
held that speculation and unverified reports do not qualify as UPSI. Options a), b), c), and e) are  
incorrect because they are expressly recognized categories of UPSI when unpublished.  
Financial results, dividend decisions, corporate expansion plans, and capital restructuring  
decisions directly affect valuation and investor behavior. Thus, market rumors remain outside  
the scope of UPSI unless officially acknowledged, making option d correct.  
21. Answer C  
Regulation 5(2) and 5(3) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 mandate  
that a trading plan shall commence only after a minimum cooling-off period of six months  
(which has now been changed to 120 days in the 2024 amendment) from the date of public  
disclosure of the plan. This safeguard prevents insiders from using near-term UPSI while  
appearing compliant. In this case, the CFO drafts a trading plan on 1st January and seeks  
commencement on 1st April, which is only three months later. This clearly violates the  
mandatory six-month cooling-off requirement. The fact that Q4 results are announced on 15th  
April further strengthens the invalidity. Option a) and b) are incorrect because the cooling-off

requirement is absolute. Option d) is incorrect as CFOs are explicitly permitted to draft trading  
plans. Option e) is incorrect because board approval cannot override statutory safeguards.

22. Answer C  
Regulation 3(1) prohibits communication, procurement, or allowing access to UPSI, except for  
legitimate purposes. However, SEBI jurisprudence clearly distinguishes mere passive receipt  
from prohibited conduct. Option c is correct because the analyst unintentionally received UPSI,  
did not trade, and did not further communicate the information. Publishing a general industry  
report, without referencing or exploiting the UPSI, does not amount to violation. Option a) and b)  
are incorrect because the regulation does not criminalize mere receipt absent misuse. Option d)  
is incorrect as analysts are not exempt from PIT regulations. Option e) is incorrect because

making option c correct.  
23. Answer C  
Under Regulation 5(5), any modification to an approved trading plan triggers a fresh cooling-off  
period of six months (which has now been changed to 120 days in the 2024 amendment).  
This ensures that insiders cannot manipulate plans opportunistically. Here, the designated  
person modified the trading plan just 10 days before execution. This modification nullifies earlier  
approval and mandates a fresh cooling-off period. As a result, trading during a closed window is  
invalid. Option a) is incorrect because trading plans override window closure only if valid. Option  
b) is incorrect because modifications are not freely permitted. Option d) is partially correct but  
incomplete; the legal defect is the cooling-off violation. Option e) is incorrect as disclosure  
cannot cure illegality. Hence, option c is correct.

Regulation 2(1)(d) treats a person as a connected person if they were associated with the  
company in the past six months and had access to UPSI. This rebuttable presumption applies to  
former employees. Since the employee resigned only 20 days earlier and had knowledge of  
merger negotiations (a classic UPSI category), she remains a connected person. Options a), c),  
d), and e) are incorrect because they misstate the statutory position. The six-month look-back is  
explicit and access-based. Thus, option b is correct.

includes gifts. Regulation 7 mandates disclosure by promoters when transaction value exceeds  
₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter. Option c is correct because gifting ₹18 lakh worth of shares  
crosses the disclosure threshold. SEBI has repeatedly clarified that gifts are not exempt.

26. Answer B  
The SEBI regulatory sandbox framework was introduced to allow regulated entities to test  
innovative products, services, or business models in a controlled environment with temporary  
regulatory relaxations. Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015,  
particularly read with Regulation 31A and SEBI’s sandbox circulars, SEBI is empowered to grant  
specific, conditional exemptions from certain regulatory requirements, including those related to  
data sharing, provided investor protection and market integrity are not compromised. In this  
scenario, the listed company is formally admitted into the sandbox for testing algorithmic  
advisory services. If SEBI has expressly permitted the sharing of live client data as part of  
sandbox conditions, such sharing is lawful, even though it may otherwise raise concerns under  
insider trading or confidentiality norms. The exemption operates only to the extent granted and  
does not amount to a blanket override of PIT regulations. Option a is incorrect because UPSI  
sharing is not “always” prohibited, SEBI can allow it through exemptions. Option c is incorrect  
because the sandbox does not override PIT automatically; permissions are conditional and  
limited. Option d is incorrect because client consent alone cannot substitute SEBI’s regulatory  
exemption. Option e is incorrect because sandbox participation is not limited only to  
intermediaries; listed companies may also participate. Thus, sandbox exemption granted by  
SEBI legitimizes the sharing, making option b correct.  
27. Answer C  
Under Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015,  
communication of UPSI is strictly prohibited, except where it is in furtherance of legitimate  
purposes, performance of duties, or discharge of legal obligations. While merchant bankers are  
permitted recipients of UPSI in transactions like rights issues, selective sharing with potential  
investors before public disclosure is not automatically a legitimate purpose. Financial projections  
shared privately with institutional investors before public announcement amount to selective  
disclosure, which undermines market equality and price discovery. SEBI has consistently held  
that investor briefings containing UPSI before public dissemination violate PIT norms,  
regardless of investor sophistication. Option a is incorrect because an NDA does not legalize  
selective disclosure. Option b is incorrect because “legitimate purpose” does not extend to  
pre-marketing to investors unless mandated by law. Option d is incorrect as merchant bankers  
are not exempt from PIT. Option e is incorrect because board approval cannot override statutory  
prohibitions. Therefore, selective sharing of UPSI with investors is prohibited, making option c  
correct.  
28. Answer B  
The concept of “generally available information” under Regulation 2(1)(e) requires that  
information be accessible to the public on a non-discriminatory basis, without barriers such as  
selective access or payment restrictions that materially limit availability. SEBI has clarified that  
information behind paywalls, proprietary databases, or restricted subscriptions does not  
automatically qualify as generally available. In this case, the designated person relied on

Insider trading prohibitions are not confined strictly to the entity to which UPSI directly pertains.  
Regulation 2(1)(n) defines UPSI broadly to include any information that, if made public, is likely  
to materially affect the price of securities. A slump sale at the parent level can significantly affect  
the financial position, operations, or valuation of a listed subsidiary, especially where  
interdependence exists. The subsidiary CEO, by virtue of his position, is a connected person  
and, upon receiving UPSI regarding the parent’s slump sale, becomes an insider for PIT  
purposes. Trading in the subsidiary’s securities while in possession of such information is  
prohibited if the information is price sensitive to the subsidiary, even indirectly. Option a is  
incorrect because material indirect impact is sufficient. Option c is incorrect because connection  
is functional, not limited to board membership. Option d is incorrect as disclosure timing does  
not legalize insider trading. Option e is incorrect because PIT regulations apply across corporate  
groups where price impact exists. Thus, option b is correct.  
30. Answer D  
Regulation 2(1)(c) mandates that a Compliance Officer must be formally appointed, financially  
literate, senior, and empowered. Regulation 9 requires the company to frame and enforce an  
effective code of conduct. Temporary absence of the Compliance Officer does not suspend  
compliance obligations. In this case, the CFO informally assumed compliance functions without  
written delegation or board authorization, rendering approvals legally invalid. The company  
failed to ensure continuity of compliance mechanisms, and the CFO exceeded authority. Option  
a is incorrect because liability extends beyond the trader. Option b is incomplete because the  
company bears primary compliance responsibility. Option c is incorrect as individual culpability  
also arises. Option e is incorrect because informal approvals have no legal standing. Thus, both  
the CFO and the company are liable, making option d correct.

possession of UPSI). The banker also violates the regulations by failing to restrict access on a

obtained before initiating the trade, not retrospectively. Here, the designated person placed the

pre-clearance. Options a and c are incorrect because timing of execution is irrelevant. Option d  
is incorrect as liability primarily rests with the trader. Option e is incorrect because PIT is a

decisions to be rule-based, transparent, and consistent with the code of conduct. Arbitrary  
refusal based on subjective “speculation risk” without UPSI or code-based justification exceeds  
authority. Option a is incorrect because discretion is regulated. Option c is incorrect because  
refusal may be justified on valid grounds. Option d is incorrect as mere possibility is insufficient.  
Option e is incorrect because board approval is not a substitute for legality. Therefore, option b

securities to which the UPSI relates. If the acquirer receives UPSI about one company but  
trades in another listed group company without a material connection, the prohibition does not  
automatically apply. Option a is incorrect because PIT is not market-wide. Option c is incorrect

is not absolute across the group. Option e is incorrect as lawful receipt does not alter scope.

36. Answer A  
Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, the concept of aggregation of  
trades is central to preventing circumvention of trading limits through relatives. Regulation 2(1)(f)  
defines immediate relatives (including spouse) as persons who are presumed to be financially  
dependent or to consult the insider in trading decisions, unless the contrary is proved.  
Consequently, under Schedule B (Code of Conduct), trades executed by a designated person  
and their immediate relatives are required to be aggregated for the purpose of determining  
thresholds for pre-clearance and disclosures. In the present scenario, although the designated  
person traded ₹10 lakh and the spouse traded ₹11 lakh separately, each appearing to fall below  
the threshold individually, the combined value of ₹21 lakh exceeds the threshold applicable  
under the company’s code of conduct. SEBI has consistently emphasized that individual  
fragmentation of trades cannot be used to bypass compliance requirements, especially where  
immediate relatives are involved. Treating spouses as “joint DPs” for threshold calculation  
ensures that insider trading controls remain effective and not merely formalistic. Option b is  
incorrect because it ignores the deeming fiction applied to immediate relatives. Option c is  
incorrect because immediate relative status flows from the regulations, not annual declarations.  
Option d is incorrect because aggregation is not limited to “acting in concert”; it is automatic  
unless rebutted. Option e is incorrect because spouses are not treated as independent for  
threshold computation. Hence, pre-clearance is required due to aggregation, making Answer A  
correct.  
37. Answer C  
Insider trading liability under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 is  
fundamentally possession-based, not status-based. Regulation 2(1)(g) defines an insider as any  
person who is either a connected person or is in possession of or has access to UPSI.  
Therefore, even a temporary consultant, engaged for only 15 days, becomes an insider the  
moment he accesses UPSI during valuation work. In this case, the consultant accessed UPSI  
during his engagement and later traded based on memory of that UPSI. The termination of the  
contract does not erase insider status for the purpose of that information. SEBI jurisprudence  
clearly establishes that once a person has been in possession of UPSI, they are prohibited from  
trading until that information becomes generally available, regardless of employment duration or  
contractual status. Option a is incorrect because insider status does not vanish immediately  
upon termination. Option b is partially misleading—while connected-person presumptions  
extend for six months, possession of UPSI alone is sufficient even without relying on  
connected-person status. Option d would apply only if UPSI had become public, which is not  
stated here. Option e is irrelevant; payment has no bearing on insider liability. Therefore, trading  
based on previously accessed UPSI constitutes a violation, making Answer C correct.  
38. Answer B  
Regulation 3(1) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 permits  
communication of UPSI only when it is in furtherance of legitimate purposes, performance of

Encumbrance creation on shares, such as pledging, is governed primarily by the SEBI  
(Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 (SAST), not by the SEBI  
(Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. PIT Regulations focus on trading based on  
UPSI, whereas encumbrances are treated as ownership and control-related disclosures, not  
insider trading events. SEBI has clarified through regulations and circulars that disclosures of  
encumbrances by promoters or designated persons must comply with Regulation 31 of SAST,  
which prescribes specific timelines. PIT Regulations do not impose disclosure obligations for  
encumbrances unless the encumbrance itself is part of a larger insider trading scheme (which is  
not alleged here). Option a is incorrect because the 2-day timeline applies to trading disclosures  
under PIT, not encumbrances. Option b is partially true but incomplete. Option c is incorrect  
because encumbrances are not treated as trades under PIT. Option e is incorrect because there  
is no overlap in timelines, each regulation operates in its own field. Therefore, only SAST  
disclosure requirements apply, making Answer D correct.  
40. Answer B  
Trading plans under Regulation 5 of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015  
are designed to allow insiders to trade in a pre-scheduled, transparent, and UPSI-neutral  
manner. While trading plans may be modified, SEBI has imposed strict safeguards to prevent  
abuse. Any modification is treated as a fresh trading plan, triggering all original conditions anew,  
including the minimum 6-month cooling-off period and the requirement that trades must not  
overlap with periods when UPSI exists. In this scenario, the fund manager modified the plan  
after two months, shifting trades into a period overlapping UPSI. This violates the very  
foundation of trading plans, which is insulation from insider knowledge. Market volatility is not a  
valid justification to override statutory safeguards. Option a is incorrect because modifications  
are permitted, subject to conditions. Option c is incorrect because shareholder approval is not  
contemplated. Option d is incorrect because UPSI overlap invalidates the plan. Option e is  
incorrect because trading plans do not lapse automatically; they become non-compliant if

conditions are breached. Accordingly, modification is allowed only if full compliance is  
maintained, making Answer B correct.
